about: How to tell if a video is AI. Factory #21, backlog row 23, playlist How tech works. Packaging 6/6. One hard idea: the glitches people hunt for (extra fingers, garbled text, shadows pointing the wrong way) are getting harder to spot, and in a 2024 study people did about as well as chance, so the check that still works is the source: who posted it first, the original upload, and an AI label or Content Credentials, while a missing label proves nothing. Sources, all read 2026-11-04: Kamali, Groh et al., 'How to Distinguish AI-Generated Images from Authentic Photographs' (Northwestern Kellogg, arXiv 2406.08651, June 2024): 'missing fingers, extra fingers, merged fingers'; text with 'nonexistent words, spelling errors'; 'shadows cast in inconsistent directions'; 'Text in AI image generation is an area that is rapidly improving and these artifacts may not always be noticeable at first glance'; reverse image search 'may trace you back to the original source'. Cooke et al., 'As Good As A Coin Toss' (CSIS, arXiv 2403.16760, 2024; 1,276 participants): 'mean detection performance close to a chance level performance of 50%'. NIST AI 100-4 (Nov 2024): 'humans may find detection more difficult as synthetic content generation continues to increase in sophistication'; metadata 'can similarly be stripped altogether, as it often is when files are shared'. YouTube Help 'Disclosing use of GenAI content': labels from creator disclosure, 'Content that contains C2PA metadata', and internal detection. TikTok newsroom (May 9, 2024): auto-labels AIGC by reading Content Credentials. Every 'AI video' in the film is drawn by hand: no real AI footage, no real faces, no real logos or app UI. Hero: the paper loupe slides off the pixels onto the poster's name tag, coral stamp WHO POSTED IT? in the 1.2 s silence after 'first.' No AI tag anywhere (Isac, 2026-11-03). dur is the chain estimate; Ming reads about 15 % faster, so expect about 31-32 s.
